title: Rome taxed urine, and its emperor said money doesn’t stink
body: Ancient Rome’s public urinals were a resource. Launderers bought the urine and let it stand until it turned into ammonia, which lifted grease from woollen togas and kept them white, and tanners used it to soften hides. Around 70 AD, Emperor Vespasian put a tax on this trade to refill a treasury drained by a year of civil war. When his son Titus objected that the money was disgusting, Vespasian held a coin to his nose and asked whether it smelled. The exchange, as Suetonius tells it, gave Latin the saying **pecunia non olet**: money doesn’t stink.

slides.heading: What urine was for
items: Cleaning: stale urine breaks down into ammonia, an alkali that lifts grease out of wool
Whitening: launderers soaked togas in it to keep them bright
Tanning: it loosened hair and softened animal hides

steps.label: Public urinals collect the city’s urine
Left to stand, it turns into ammonia
Ammonia lifts grease: togas come out white
Vespasian taxes the trade, c. AD 70

slides.attribution: Vespasian, holding a coin from the tax under his son Titus’s nose (Suetonius)

slides.heading: A tax with history
slides.text: Nero had tried a urine tax first, the vectigal urinae, and it was dropped. Vespasian revived it, and it was the buyers of the urine who paid, not the citizens who, so to speak, supplied the goods.

slides.heading: Still with us
slides.text: Two thousand years on, public urinals in Italy are vespasiani and in France vespasiennes, and ‘money doesn’t stink’ is still the shrug of anyone taking cash from an unglamorous source.

slides.question: Who actually paid Vespasian’s urine tax?
options: The buyers who collected the urine
slides.explanation: The tax fell on the trade: the fullers and tanners who bought urine from the public urinals paid it.

slides.heading: Who did what?
slides.explanation: Nero’s vectigal urinae was dropped; Vespasian brought it back around AD 70; his son Titus objected; and the biographer Suetonius preserved the exchange.
